args.text:
There's no such thing as a safe spot outside when there's thunderstorms about. Hear thunder, and chances are yer within strikin' distance of the storm. Just remember, “When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!” Too many people leave it way too late to get somewhere safe when a thunderstorm's rollin' in. And sadly, leavin' it late is what's behind a lot of the lightnin' deaths and injuries in the U.S.

Best way to look after yerself with lightnin'? Don't be anywhere near it. Ya just don't wanna get caught out in a storm, simple as that. Have a lightnin' safety plan, and if thunderstorms are forecast, pull the pin on things or put 'em off early. Keep an eye on the weather and get yerself somewhere safe before it turns nasty. A solid building or a car with a hard roof is a safe bet. Rain shelters, little sheds and open vehicles aren't.

Once yer inside, don't touch anythin' plugged into a power point, don't touch the plumbin', and don't touch a phone with a cord on it. Mobiles and cordless phones are right. Keep away from outside doors and windows too, and don't go lyin' on a garage floor.

Gettin' Yer Head Round the Threat

Whether someone cops a lightnin' strike comes down to how they carry on when thunderstorms are about. The graphs below give ya a squiz at why and when people get struck, and what they can do to cut their risk.

In the first graph, the threat of lightnin' climbs as a thunderstorm rolls in, peaks when the storm's right overhead, then slowly tapers off as it moves away. But it's how people carry on that decides the risk of a deadly strike. Some head inside at the first sign of a thunderstorm, but heaps leave it way too late to get somewhere safe. Some hang about till the storm's right overhead and the rain's started. Others haven't planned ahead, so they get caught outside with nowhere safe to get to. Most people do make it inside, but then some put themselves at risk by touchin' things that could get electrified if lightnin' hits nearby. And last of all, heaps of people head back out too soon after the storm looks to have gone through, often only waitin' till the rain eases off or stops. It's all of that, every one of those unsafe habits, that puts people at risk when thunderstorms are about.

Cuttin' the Risk

To keep yer own risk of gettin' hit as low as it'll go, plan ahead when ya head outside, so ya can get somewhere safe quick smart if a thunderstorm's brewin'. If the sky's lookin' nasty or ya hear thunder, get inside somewhere safe straight away. Once yer in, keep off phones with a cord, electrical gear and the plumbin', and keep away from windows and doors. Then wait 30 minutes after the last lightnin' or thunder before ya head back out. If every bloke and sheila stuck to those simple rules, we'd see a lot fewer lightnin' casualties in this country.

So remember, it's how you carry on when thunderstorms are about that decides yer own risk of gettin' struck by lightnin'. When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!

Lightnin' Victims

If someone's been struck by lightnin', they might need medical help straight away. A lightnin' victim doesn't carry an electrical charge, so they're safe to touch. Call 911 and keep an eye on 'em. Start CPR or use an Automated External Defibrillator if needed.
